profile: Opens a paragraph on the last one's point, often by restating it as a premise: 'If the signs are present and plain and yet we still pass them by, the fault is on our side.' / 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.'
Ends paragraphs on the point itself, often a short plain sentence rather than an aphorism: 'In most of us, it is not working.' / 'That side of the religion is called ʿirfan.'
Medium-length sentences, joined with 'and' without commas; semicolons set two halves against each other: 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them.'
Uses 'whereas' and colons for contrast and lists: 'Eyes and ears take in the surface of things, whereas inside a human being there should be something more: a faculty...'
Brings sources in once, with a varied verb, and explains the quotation straight after: 'Sheikh Bahmanpour compares this faculty to a machine... That machine is the soul.'
Names the Sheikh sparingly, and after the first mention as 'the Sheikh' / 'in the Sheikh's words'; no 'he says' filler
Stacks a second scholar only to add something: 'Mohammad Ali Shomali makes the same point, describing the obligatory rules of fiqh as...'
Inclusive 'we/us', an occasional 'Let's', almost no 'you'; never scolds: 'Most of us see only the lamp.'
Plain, concrete images: 'a person who sees a red light thinks of the danger it warns of, not of the colour and shape of the lamp'
Explicit signposting to other chapters and clear concessions: 'as Chapter One shows' / 'For the avoidance of doubt, this invitation... is not an invitation to circumvent the law'
Explains a verse by reasoning from it: 'Cattle see and hear perfectly well, so the comparison cannot be about the senses.'
Never: rhetorical questions, jokes, exclamations, closing flourishes, or saying the same thing twice in a paragraph

tells: Explains the verse straight after it ('Most of us fear Allah's punishment...'), as A does; the only weak spot is the slightly aphoristic 'Tawhid is simple to say and hard to grasp'
'Sheikh Bahmanpour reads... In his reading... the Sheikh finds both' — teacher named three times in one paragraph; A names him once and then gets on with the content
'"O Lord of Glory and Honor, (please do) make me love meeting You," it says' — 'it says' filler, and the quotation is left unexplained; A would gloss what the request means
'In this request the heart is brought near by its own passion for God.' — says again what the quoted line says without moving the argument on

'It is difficult, but it is open, because we are made for it... He means this as a statement of what we were made for... God created us with that capacity and wants us to reach it' — the same point made three times; A makes it once
'He means this as a statement of what we were made for.' — an editorial gloss that adds nothing to the Sheikh's quotation
'This is the case for pursuing ʿirfan.' — a tidy summary line; A's summaries carry the argument step by step rather than announcing it
Picks up the last point ('The circle does not mean...'), reasons from the quotation ('A book can hold the whole mind, so the mind can be held'), and signposts a later chapter, all in A's way
Tight, stepwise argument ('The law can be kept without the path... The path cannot be walked without the law, because...') with the source kept in footnotes, as in A
Opens on the last point and uses 'whereas' for contrast, as A does; a closing line close to a summary ('the real ʿarif is the one who keeps it without a break') keeps this near even

Concrete, reasoned exposition ('its colour, its size, what it does'); 'In the Sheikh's account' introduces him once; ends on the point 'God has no colour, no dimension and no function for the mind to take hold of'
'for Sheikh Bahmanpour... he says... the ʿurafaʾ say... the Sheikh adds' — attribution in nearly every sentence; A attributes once and states the content
'This light usually reaches a traveller through another heart.' — the second paragraph opens by repeating the first paragraph's opening sentence instead of moving on
'We know from experience how knowledge passes from one mind to another... we have no such experience' — more words than the point needs before the quotation that makes it
Picks up the last point ('The Prophet gave that reason himself'), explains the quotation, ties it back to the opening Munajat, then signposts Chapter Sixteen, which is A's pattern

The opening reasons from the last point ('If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works'), and the verse is explained by reasoning ('A heart trembles only at the mention of someone it has some experience of')
The chapter opening matches the reference ('These words come...'); the concrete example ('whether the car was locked') and 'That gap can lead to a tempting conclusion' pick up each point in turn
'Mutahhari also explains why seeking them would be shirk: the goal has become something other than God.' — repeats the quotation just given ('something other than God Himself') without moving on
'The scholars differ in emphasis but agree that powers are not the aim.' — a summary paragraph that restates the conclusion; A would go straight to 'With powers set aside...'
'Murtada Mutahhari uses the same word as Sheikh Bahmanpour.' — opens on the source rather than the point; A would open on the claim and then bring in Mutahhari
The opening matches the reference's way of introducing a prayer ('a prayer many of us recite'); the signposting is heavy ('Chapter Two' twice) but A signposts this way too

Plain register and the gloss on shirk fit A; the weaker points are 'must be held apart from the real thing' (slightly preachy), 'ended his first lecture more strongly' (unclear link to what came before) and the dramatic 'Then: "These are shirk."'

The quotation is explained by reasoning ('A result in the laboratory is known because it has been observed, not because it has been deduced'), much as A explains a source; the second scholar adds an image rather than just repeating the point

Uses semicolons to balance two views ('The scholars speak of how far a reciter reaches; the Sheikh speaks of who may begin'), opens the next paragraph on the last one's phrase ('Access to these words...'), and signposts the argument as A does
'Whoever abandons that order will not find the pearl.' — says again what the quotation has just said; A would move straight to the conclusion
'Kubra draws this conclusion from his own image... Kubra says' — Kubra is named three times across two paragraphs, plus 'Sheikh Bahmanpour gives an image'; A names a source once
'This is why the ʿurafaʾ say that the beginning of ʿirfan is the shariʿa.' — a tidy closing summary line
Semicolon contrasts ('Other people look at the surface of the world; the friends of God look at what lies inside it'), and the verse is followed by a plain gloss of muqarrabun, as in A
